utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could I remind you once against, General, that the affirmation still applies and we're now on the last run, I believe. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And just one brief housekeeping matter. Last evening after court the Prosecution and the Defence solemnly reflected on the video-clip that I -- that the Prosecution had shown to General Jovanovski yesterday, and this is time code 00:31:16 to 00:32:59, from Rule 65 ter 979, and we clarified yesterday that this is not Exhibit P0027, and so at this time the Prosecution would move to tender this particular video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P439, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, where we left off yesterday, we were about to look at one of the Official Notes produced during the work of your commission in 2003. But before we look at that, General, perhaps I should start, General, just focus on my question for now, please. I need to start with a more basic question. Why did the commission that you led in 2003 create records of its work and of its meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the official final document? Documents of the meetings or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm referring to everything, all the records. Why were records made?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is needed to leave a trace that we've been working something. So what has been said or what has been worked to be documented in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. So the purpose of the records was to document the work -- what the committee did. Is that fair? Okay. If we can turn to what is tab 12 of General Jovanovski's binder, and I misspoke yesterday, and unfortunately -- fortunately, my colleagues of the Defence caught my mistake. This is a document that is actually 65 ter 285.13. It's from the exhibit that's marked for identification, P00379. And I'd like to ask the usher's assistance, please. To save time, I've marked a copy of the Macedonian version, the points which I would like to direct General Jovanovski's attention. General Jovanovski, you can see that this is a document to the sector for internal affairs of the ministry of internal affairs, there's a typo in the date in the English version. It should say 19 November 2003, rather than 2001. But if you turn to the last page, General, you'll see that this is an Official Note written by Ljube Krstevski, who was the head of the department for internal affairs in Cair. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to correct you. At the time he wrote this Official Note he was not the head of SVR Cair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I -- I take your correction, you're absolutely right. In 2001, the summer of 2001, Mr. Krstevski was the head of the department for internal affairs for Cair. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljube Krstevski describes the events of 2001 in 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct. And we see in the very top paragraph in the -- take a look at the first page, General. The first page, General. The very first paragraph. Ljube Krstevski describes his appointment as head of the department for internal affairs, Cair. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can move, please, to the second page in the English version and the third page in the Macedonian version. Then I may be off by one, General. The fourth page in the Macedonian version. We'll just wait a minute for the e-court versions to come up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let us just state that the date is wrong in the translation. The Official Note says 19th of November 2003, while the translation says 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I said that a couple of minutes ago, I think, yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, I'd like to direct your attention down a little bit in the middle of the page to a passage -- this is on page 2 of the English version, and I believe now it's page 5 of the Macedonian version. It -- there's a passage where it says -- where Mr. Krstevski writes this is, and he's talking about the 10th of August after the mine explosion at Ljubotenski Bacila. And then he says: "The next day the soldiers were buried." The next day would have been the 11th of August. "At that time, I was called personally on the phone, cell phone 070243818. Minister Ljube Boskoski phoned and told me that a person by the name Johan would come to me who is in his personal security and that if he requests any services, I have orders from him to carry them out." Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to make a correction in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljube Krstevski has not been called by the minister, but here it reads that I was called on the phone by Minister Boskoski and who told me all that. So the minister called on the phone but whether the minister called on the phone that's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General for that clarification and then later on it says: "On the 11th, around 1500 hours some people in police uniforms arrived at the grounds of police station Cair about whom I later learned that they are reservists from (illegible) of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. In (illegible) of police station Cair entered Ljubomir Gjuricinovski and started to tell that Bucuk, a nickname, had arrived from people from (illegible) and he complained that they had been given uniforms and weapons." Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn now to page 3 in the English version and the next page in the Macedonian version. General, do you see on the next page there's a paragraph towards the top of the page, beginning: "That night around 1800 hours." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says this: "That night, around 1800 hours, deputy commander Stojanovski and deputy commander Bliznakovski called me and ordered me to go to a meeting with commander Slavko Ivanovski, a representative of the army of the Republic of Macedonia - I later found out it was Major Despodovski - which I refused. But I was told that I had to go in order to show -- in order to know what the intentions are of the group of Johan and Bucuk which was already on the positions in the recreation centre above village Ljuboten so that it would be regular. I took along the analytic chief Borce, the representative of defence preparations, Ilija Stefanovski and together with Commander Slavko, we went to the meeting. At the meeting, I insisted that minutes are taken which we already even started, but because of Johan, Bucuk and I think there was one more person by the nickname Kunga we could not take minutes." Have you been following with me, General?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn now, please, to page 4 in the English version and the next page in the Macedonian version. And in the English version, near the top -- near the top of the English version Mr. Krstevski is talking about the events of Sunday, the 12th of August after Minister Ljube Boskoski arrived in the Ljubanci area. And do you see there's a passage there, General, that begins: "While the minister was there." Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that's says: "While the minister was there, Johan's group was bringing around 10 captured Albanians from village (illegible) when they neared the check-point at around 50 metres, a person, reservist of the army of the Republic of Macedonia ran towards the group and hit one of the persons," et cetera. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then lower down in that paragraph, and we may need to turn the page in the Macedonian version, you see there's a sentence that says: "After 1430 hours, all persons from the unit that were led by Johan left with their (illegible) from the village Ljuboten and the recreation centre in village Ljubanci." Do you see that, General? If you go to the next page and look for the number 1430. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the number, but I can see something else written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you go a few lines below that. You'll see the number 1430 mentioned once or twice again. We're looking for a sentence that says: "After 1430 hours, all persons from the unit that was led by Johan."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. General, would you agree that Mr. Krstevski's statement to the commission in 2003 would allow the commission to determine that Mr. Tarculovski was in the village of Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when Ljube Krstevski were called for an interview in the commission, he was visually disturbed. I might say that he was even agitated. The sentences that he spoke were unrelated to one another and had no logical sequence in them. He was mixing people, mixing positions, and we just asked him to write -- to sit down and write what he knows. But it is also visible in the note that he changes his positions, because he told us one thing and then he wrote another thing in the Official Note. It is not a characteristic of a minister to call by phone and issue orders when Ljube Krstevski has his own superiors from whom he receives his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You've reviewed parts of this Official Note that we've looked at today, have you, General? Where Mr. Krstevski has written about the events of the 10th of August, the 11th of August, and the 12th of August? You've seen what we've reviewed today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, would you agree that these sentences written by Mr. Krstevski are in a logical sequence and are related to each other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly because of that, these persons mentioned here were called and they were interviewed and we were not able to determine from those interviews that they have been present at the certain place at a certain time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand you correctly, based on the information that Mr. Krstevski gave to the 2003 commission, the commission decided to interview or speak with additional persons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only from Mr. Krstevski's note but also from all the interviews with the persons listed in the final report of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You say it is not a characteristic of a minister to call by phone and issue orders. Actually, I'll come back to that in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness, please, what is Exhibit P00072. Before we get to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovski, would you agree that there's no record -- there's no information in any of the records of the committee that you led in 2003 indicating that Mr. Krstevski seemed agitated when he spoke to the committee. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If you take a look, please, at this document on the screen in front of you, General. It's dated the 6th of July, 2001, from the Ministry of the Interior. And you'll see this is a decision appointing Ljube Krstevski as the head of the department of the Ministry of the Interior, Cair, beginning on the 1st of August, 2001. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move down so that we can see the bottom of each page, please. Perhaps can we, please, go to the next page in each version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see, General, that at the end of this document we see this decision is signed by Ljube Boskoski, then the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly now, according pursuant to which law or which rule. An employer in the ministry is the minister. The minister is the one who signs all the decisions to hire or to fire someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, back in August 2001, Ljube Krstevski was the head of OVR Cair, and can we agree that the village of Ljuboten fell within the authority of OVR Cair?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is Prosecution Rule 65 ter 232, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see, General, this is a document dated the 12th of August, 2001. It's the report on registered events and measures undertaken as part of Operation Ramno. And can we scroll down so that we can see the bottom of each page, please. And if we could go to the next page in the Macedonian version, just in the Macedonian version. You see, General, this is a report sent by Ljube Krstevski on the 12th of August during which he's talking about -- or he is relaying information related to the Ljubanci and Ljuboten area. Do you -- have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page in the Macedonian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see that: "At 1040 hours shots and detonations could be heard from the upper part of Ljuboten village, along the road to Rastak. A number of houses were burning and the movement of eight to ten individuals was noticed around them." Do you see that, General, in the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, but I don't see there a registration number or a signature of the person, of the head, and I'm not sure whether the head have seen this document at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, that may be. Can you see down below that the -- it says: "At 1540 hours the Ljubanci check-point reported that 100 people were noticed at MV Buzalak walking along the ridge." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: As head of the Ministry of Interior for OVR Cair was it part of Ljube Krstevski's duties to compile such information and report it up his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P440, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Jovanovski, can you think of a reason why the commission formed by Minister Boskoski in August 2001 could not have interviewed Ljube Krstevski?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment about the work of the first commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know you didn't work on the first commission, but I'm simply asking you in your opinion, can you think of a reason why that first commission could not have interviewed Ljube Krstevski?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it -- the right question for the witness might be whether the witness knows if the first commission interviewed Ljube Krstevski, not to offer a response immediately, a response that was not based in the questions up to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point is that the first step has not yet been clarified by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Jovanovski, do you know whether the commission established by Minister Boskoski in 2001 interviewed Ljube Krstevski?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Today -- excuse me, yesterday you told the Trial Chamber that the situation for the police was much more difficult in 2001 than in 2003 due to problems that the police had returning to the crisis areas. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was it very difficult in 2001 for members of the Ministry of the Interior to speak with police officers who worked in police stations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't understand your question. Who -- to speak with whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if members of the Ministry of the -- members of the Ministry of Interior, criminal inspectors or other members of the ministry or the police wanted to inquire about events that occurred within police stations in Macedonia during 2001, was such a -- such an activity, such an inquiry very difficult?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a bit more difficult to work in 2001 and to inquire among colleagues because they had extended working hours and they had less time to rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So that would have meant that the colleague would have been on duty for longer periods of time in 2001, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so at least some of those colleagues who worked in police stations would have been easier to locate, isn't that correct, because they would have been spending more time at their place of work?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not predominantly in the police stations. They were predominantly at the check-points and patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But, of course, if they were at check-points or patrolling, their commanders would know where they were. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Last week at page 4869 of the transcript, Ms. Residovic asked you whether Minister Boskoski fully respected the opinions, suggestions and recommendations of his directors and under-secretaries. And it appears that, from the transcript, in response to that question, you said: "That was not a great virtue of his, but he always asked us to have the last word on a matter." Do you remember that exchange?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the conversation, but I don't remember that I provided this specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was always the last word would be given by us professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the last part of the sentence is correct, but the first part of the sentence, I don't remember if I have spoken such words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. After you and your colleagues at the collegium would have the last word on a discussion or a debate about a matter, would it be then up to Minister Boskoski to make a decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After we agree, then this is all agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And then -- all right. I will -- I will leave that there. At page 4876 you told Ms. Residovic that there was no need for the minister to check or corroborate information that he received from you. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question, because the translation somehow ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question was: Last week at page 4876 of the transcript, you told Ms. Residovic and the Chamber that there was no need for the minister, Minister Boskoski, to check or corroborate information that he received from you and your colleagues. Do you recall that exchange?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question is: If the minister believed that he needed more information about a particular issue, could the minister have ordered one of his subordinates - you or someone else - to obtain more information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me, but the directors. The direct subordinates would be the directors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So then if Minister Boskoski believed that he needed some more information, then Minister Boskoski could have ordered one of his directors to try to obtain more information, and then those orders would be passed down the chain of command. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in 2001, did the minister -- did Minister Boskoski issue or give such orders, when appropriate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a general question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A few minutes ago we were talking about the meetings of the collegium and discussions that occurred there, and you told the Chamber that after we agreed, then this is all agreed. After these discussions and a consensus is formed about a particular matter, would then Minister Boskoski issue tasks or instructions or orders to his directors, based on what was agreed, based on the consensus that had been reached?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the agreement, I don't remember that he would comment additionally during the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But he could issue orders related to agreements or consensus that were reached at the collegium, right? He had that authority.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN JOVANOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that besides his immediate subordinates, during the meetings he can ask from his director any type -- for any type of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. You will be pleased to learn, General, that that concludes the questions to be asked of you, so your evidence is at an end. The Chamber would express its appreciation of your assistance and for your having come to The Hague to assist in this trial. You may, of course, now return to your normal activities and the court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution would seek to tender the documents that are included in what has been marked for identification as P00379. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm afraid we have a few objection in relation to a number of documents which form part of this package. Perhaps I will let Mr. Saxon finish, if that is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm perfectly willing to listen to the objections and respond to them if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in that case there are two sets of objections concerning partly overlapping documents and I will identify the two sets of objection. The first set of objection concerns material which pertains more specifically to information provided by co-accused, co-defendant Mr. Johan Tarculovski to the second commission and I will identify those for the record by their number. The first one is Rule 65 ter 285.6, which is part of MFI 379. The second is 285.7 and it is also 285.19, again part of 379. Rule 65 ter 285.10, which is also 285.22, 285.24 which is also 285.25, and we understand that Mr. Saxon would or might also seek to tender what is MFI'd as P51. The second set of objections, Your Honour, applies to those documents as well as a number of other proposed exhibits and I would also identify them for the record. This is 285.11, which is also 285.23, 285.14, 285.1, 285.2, 285.3, which is also 285.15. 285.6 which is also 285.18, MFI P435, 65 ter 285.12, and 285.13. Concerning the first set of documents, Your Honour, that those are the documents which contain information attributed to Mr. Tarculovski and given to the second commission. The Defence submit that should this evidence be admitted the -- the Defence would be prejudiced in this case, since it cannot compel Mr. Tarculovski to appear as a witness and therefore, cannot test the reliability or otherwise of this material and information. In other words, the Defence is unable to confront the evidence which, in turn, would violate the fundamental right of Mr. Boskoski to confront evidence which may be relevant to his case. Furthermore, and even if the Defence had the right to compel Mr. Tarculovski, which we understand we don't, Mr. Tarculovski will have the right to remain silent which, in effect, would lead to the same result, the Defence being unable to exercise its right to confront the evidence. Furthermore, and as indicated during the evidence of both Ms. Groseva and Mr. Jovanovski which we have just heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you may need to slow down a little Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I think it's a fair warning, Your Honour. I may be in trouble with the interpreters, otherwise. The second basis we submit for the non-admission of the first set of document was that during two of the three sessions at which Mr. Tarculovski was heard by the commission, he was unrepresented and Rule 42(A)(i) would as a result have been violated. The Tribunal has had occasion to point out that Rule 42 applies not only to interviews conducted by the Office of the Prosecutor but also by any other authority. And perhaps to save a bit of time I will not read the passage in question, but simply indicate for Your Honours' assistance a decision of the Trial Chamber in the Delalic and other case of the 2nd of September of 1997, in particular paragraph 43 which refers and turns to Article 14.3 of the ICCPR and Article 63(C) of the ECHR as a basis for its ruling. This is the decision of Zdravo Mucic motion for the exclusion of evidence. The same point is being made in Article 551(C) of the ICC statute which, in effect, has adopted the approach of the Trial Chamber in this case. The other reason or one other reason in any case for which the material pertaining to Mr. Tarculovski should not be admitted is the indication given by the witnesses, again Ms. Groseva and Mr. Jovanovski, that Mr. Tarculovski was not -- was not given the warning provided for in Article 42, Rule 42(A)(iii) of our Rules which requires that the suspect or the person who should be regarded as such should be given the warning that the material in question should be -- could be used against him in further proceedings. I will also draw Your Honours's attention to the statement of the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal which noted the following. A prerequisite for admission of evidence must be compliance by the moving party with any relevant safeguards and procedural protection and that it must be shown that the relevant evidence is reliable. This is Kvocka Appeals Chamber judgement 28th of February, 2005, paragraph 128. The same point was made by the Celebici Appeals Chamber in its judgement at paragraph 533. The consequence of the failure to comply with Rule 42 has again been highlighted by the Trial Chamber in the Delalic case, the same decision that I mentioned earlier and I will again cite from the decision itself. It says this: "It seems to us extremely difficult for a statement taken in violation of Rule 42 to follow within Rule 95 which protects the integrity of the proceedings by the non-admissibility of evidence obtained by method which casts substantial doubt on its reliability." And, Your Honour, the third point which specifically applies in that context to the material provided by Mr. Tarculovski to the commission is its general lack of reliability. This point has been made quite clearly by both Ms. Groseva and certainly by General Jovanovski to the effect that the material was regarded by them as being unreliable. We understand that the Prosecution has not taken this issue in re-examination in any case as pertaining to the assessment made by General Jovanovski in that respect. We understand that a finding as to the reliability or otherwise is to be made by the Trial Chamber and not by the witness. However, we believe that the view of the members of the commission who took down that evidence or information provided by Mr. Tarculovski in those circumstances is highly relevant to assessing its reliability or otherwise. And there again, Your Honour, we are back to the original problem or issue which we mentioned at the beginning is the inability or impossibility for the Defence of Mr. Boskoski to compel Mr. Tarculovski with a view to test this evidence. Concerning the second set of documents, Your Honour, and there again the submissions I'm going to make will also apply to the material which Mr. Tarculovski has provided to the commission. There's a number of additional evidence, but I will start, if I may, with the -- an objection which applies specifically to document 285.6, which is also 285.18, which contains information which was provided by Mr. Krstevski, Mr. Jovanovski, Bucuk, by Mr. Bliznakovski and by Mr. Stojanovski. All of these individuals have at one point or another been interviewed by the Prosecution or been regarded by the Prosecution as suspects in this case. As such they should have been given the rights, we submit, of Rule 42. And they haven't in those circumstances as we've seen the Rules have not been respected. And even if, as may be submitted, the Rule 42 would not apply to persons which are not defendants in a particular case we would submit that the failure of the commission to guarantee those rights would be highly relevant to the reliability or otherwise of the material provided by these people. Again, the individuals who testified before the commissions were not offered the rights to be represented or, in any case, we have no evidence of that in relation to these people. They were not given the right to remain silent, they were not informed that the material in question could be used in the context of criminal proceedings. The material, or the proceedings, we call them that, were not in any way subjected to any sort of judicial oversight which we suggest is relevant. I will also make a general point which has been made in evidence through both Ms. Groseva and Mr. Jovanovski is that material collected by the commission would not be admissible in evidence before Macedonian courts because of the nature of the process and the lack of guarantees. We understand that this in itself would not be sufficient to exclude the material from admission in this Tribunal which has its own rules of admission of evidence. We submit, however, that this is once again an indication of the care with which this material should be handled and the general lack of reliability thereof. Reliability, again, Your Honour, a number of factor which we submit is very relevant to the issue of reliability is the fact that these interviews were neither audio or videotaped that. Records are not in any way verbatim records of what was said, that they are merely summary taken by various individuals and at the time, as we've understood, written down by some of the individuals who were heard by the commission. The witnesses have also indicated significant differences between the different versions given by the witness even within one single document. The witnesses have also indicated that truth or otherwise of the information contained therein was not in any way verified by the commission. The statements or informations were not taken under oath there was no warning and no sanction of any risk of perjury, in other words, the persons heard by the commission did not have any obligation and were not in any way told that they had an obligation to tell the truth. For some of them, Your Honour, there may have been good reason to lie to the commission. We will also indicate that in our view, in the submission of the Defence, the material in question would be incapable of establishing the truth of its content. The Prosecution has made the point last week that to the extent that a party should seek to prove a fact evidence should be called on that point. We believe that this would certainly apply in this particular instance and that the only fact that would have been proved by those record is the fact that these individuals were heard by the commission and that they gave a particular version to the commission. We submit, however, that the material is incapable of proving the truth of its content. There are other submissions in relation to MFI 251, Rule 65 ter 285.1, 285.2, 285.3, 285.13, Your Honour. All of those documents are, in effect, letter exchanged between the Prosecution and one particular member of the commission, Mr. Besim Ramicevic. Your Honour, last week ruled in relation to two proposed documents of the Defence that those, in effect -- I apologise, that those documents, in effect, could not be admitted as exhibits following an objection of my colleague Mr. Saxon on that point. We would make the exact same point in relation to these four documents. For all purposes those documents should be regarded as statements of the persons signing them and as such, cannot be admitted as exhibits. Concerning MFI 251, we will also indicate at this stage that during the evidence of both Mr. Jovanovski, General Jovanovski and Ms. Groseva, the document has been said to be unreliable in several ways and was prepared and provided to the Prosecution in violations of the rules or the principle which was applicable to the commission. Again, Your Honour, we are not suggesting that in itself would be a basis sufficient to exclude this document, but again we believe that this would be relevant to assess the reliability of this document. Finally, I will make submission in relation to document 285.13, which we understand Mr. Saxon is also seeking to tender. This is one of the last documents showed to General Jovanovski. It is a note written down by one of the proposed (redacted) In relation to this particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not immediately persuaded that there is need. Unless Mr. Mettraux is going to say something beyond my expectation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would be surprised if I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the name of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A name of someone who has received protective measures from this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my colleague and I apologise, Your Honour. Concerning the evidence of this particular individual, Your Honour, we would like to indicate that -- well, perhaps we should move into private session then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon was well ahead of us. Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would also indicate that the points made earlier in submissions concerning the reliability of the material should not solely be regarded, we submit, as a matter of weight but as a matter of admission. We submit that the material in question is so unreliable that the Chamber should take the view in this particular instance that the material should not be admitted and that it should not simply be regarded as a matter of weight. There are two other matters which I simply note for the record as I understand that my colleague Mr. Apostolski may want to consider in relation to the submissions for his client, Mr. Tarculovski, but which are also relevant to the Defence of Mr. Boskoski is the fact that obviously Mr. Tarculovski has a right not to incriminate himself and that he has a right to remain silent which, again, may be a factor relevant to Your Honours decision as regards the admission of material pertaining to him. In view of the submissions, we would submit that pursuant to Article 21 of the statute, 89, 95 and 42 of the Rules, Your Honour, the documents which were identified at the beginning should not be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mettraux. Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I fully support the objection by my co-counsel Mr. Mettraux and to this Chamber I would like to point out a few more elements. Although we know that this Tribunal has its own rules for admissibility of evidence, I would like to point out to the Chamber that on the basis of the evidence collected in this manner refer -- related to the operation of the commission, a decision by a Macedonian court cannot be based on it, and they cannot be presented as evidence in the criminal procedure before the courts in the Republic of Macedonia. And that is why I believe that this kind of evidence should not be admitted by this Court. In this manner, the Macedonian law provides protection for the fundamental human rights and we believe that this Court should also protect the human rights at least to the same extent as it is being done by the Macedonian law. Also I would like to point out that at the period when the statement by Mr. Tarculovski was taken by the commission, the ICTY Prosecution office was already in charge of the Ljuboten case and that is why the -- taking the deposition would be a bypass of the rules determined in Rule 42 of the Rule Book and this would be a -- presented that this Court takes a certain documents as evidence without telling the accused his rights. Mr. Tarculovski, when he was giving his statement, was not warned about his right to keep silent, and he was not represented by a lawyer during these interviews which would mean that Rule 42 was violated. Thank you very much, Your Honours, and I would propose for this kind of evidence not to be admitted by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tarculovski -- your client, I think, is -- continues to be either embarrassed or flattered. I apologise, Mr. Apostolski. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution, in order to save time, reduced its submissions today has produced a skeleton argument of its arguments on this matter, and we have copies for everyone here today. We would like to distribute them now to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is a skeleton with some substance still on the bone, by the look.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll explain. I will explain the contents of it, Your Honour, but we're not going to review all of it today, unless the Chamber wants me to. The first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate that the Chamber is moving toward a view that in view of some of the matters raised, it could be useful to have in the end a written outline from all parties. That doesn't mean that we will not value brief oral submissions now to help us focus, but I think all counsel can appreciate that, as the matter is presented by Mr. Mettraux and Mr. Apostolski, there are some significant issues that need to be determined and which will have effects beyond this particular case. So make your submissions, but bear in mind that they will need to be consolidated into a written submission to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly, the -- most of the first page of this skeleton argument simply refers to the applicable rules and applicable jurisprudence on this matter. Most of the jurisprudence actually has been already mentioned by my colleague Mr. Mettraux, most but not all of it. There's a decision also from this Trial Chamber in the Mrkisic trial and a decision from the Prlic Trial Chamber that are also relevant to the issues that are now before the Chamber related to this evidence. Your Honour, in respect though to decision that the Trial Chamber must make, first of all, the determination as to whether this material is relevant will clear -- the Prosecution submits that the relevance of the material is obvious. And that, then, leaves two more questions for the Trial Chamber to review: Were these materials obtained under any form of oppression or coercion and are these materials reliable. And if you turn to page 2 of the skeleton argument, you'll see the Prosecution submissions that with references to the transcript that there's no evidence that any of this information was provided to the 2003 commission under oppression or any form of coercion. And we have several comments from both witnesses Tatjana Groseva and General Zoran Jovanovski on this matter. Moving on, Your Honour, the evidence of Mr. Groseva and General Zoran Jovanovski actually demonstrates that the material produced by the 2003 commission is reliable. Both witnesses talked about how the work was -- the work of the commission was performed, and how the records of the commission and its work and its discussions were recorded. And if I can particularly direct your attention to the fact that, with respect to one of the -- one of the minutes related to Johan Tarculovski, the minutes that Mr. Tarculovski and General Jovanovski signed on the 12th of November, 2003. Both General Jovanovski and Mr. Tarculovski who was assisted at the time by counsel had the opportunity to review them prior to signing them. That's at page -- pages 47229 and 4844 of the transcript. Your Honour, attached to our skeleton argument we have -- is a corroboration chart. If you turn to the fourth page of the materials that are stapled together there. And what the Prosecution has done is created a chart with respect to the primary documents that are contained within exhibit marked for identification 379 that shows for each document where there is already admitted evidence corroborating the materials, the particular material produced by the 2003 commission. And if you could turn to the fourth page of the corroboration chart, one of the -- there is the interview provided by Mr. Tarculovski on the 6th of May, 2003. And you will see there is a blank box next to the statement that Minister Boskoski gave Mr. Tarculovski a verbal order to solve the situation in Ljuboten. Your Honour, the Prosecution has left that box blank because to date there is no admitted evidence that would corroborate that statement of Mr. Tarculovski. However, I simply want to bring to the attention of Your Honours that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say that at least one Judge has got each alternate page only of the written outline or skeleton.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I appear to have all pages. That's an undue favouritism, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: I would appreciate to have the even numbers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Walpita, do you have an extra full copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two extra.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two extra full copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would appreciate one, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may prove to be a good thing that we anticipated written submissions, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It may well be, Your Honour. I will simply remark that there is some corroboration of the statement of Johan Tarculovski that he received an order from Minister Boskoski to solve the situation in Ljuboten. That corroboration is provided in the Official Note written by Ljube Krstevski, which is part of P00379. It has not yet been admitted. With respect to the admissibility of 251, what has been marked for identification of Exhibit P00251, and again, when you have the full copy of our corroboration chart, and as well on this page 3 of the skeleton argument you will see that Witness M-053, confirmed the information contained in Exhibit P251. And Witness Tatjana Groseva at page 4738, confirmed that the information contained in the commission's report, reports, dated 6th of May and 28 May, 2003 are similar to that in P -- or similar to that in Exhibit P00251. My learned colleague has argued that P00251 should not be admitted because it is effectively a letter from a member of the Ministry of the Interior, but the Prosecution would suggest that the corroboration of the material contained in exhibit 251 distinguishes it from other such letters provided by the Macedonian government and would, therefore, argue that it is admissible in this case. Can we go into private session, please for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just finally and briefly, Your Honour, the -- my colleagues raise the argument that several of the persons who were interviewed by the 2003 commission were subsequently treated as suspects by the Office of the Prosecutor. Again, Your Honour, the Prosecution feels that this is really beside the point. The point is that we have a situation here that -- to the Prosecution's knowledge is not covered specifically by any of the Rules or specifically by any of the jurisprudence. We have a situation where what is effectively an internal administrative proceeding was taking place over some months in 2003 under the auspices of the Macedonian Ministry of the Interior. So then again, the issue then is whether these documents have sufficient reliability to show their probative value so that they can be admitted at this time. And in the Prosecution's submission, when you have our full corroboration chart and our full outline, if we are ordered to produce one, then these documents are admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux and Mr. Apostolski, in view of the now firmed view of the Chamber that there should be written submissions, it would seem unnecessary to call on you for a reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. That being so, the Chamber would thank counsel for their interesting submissions. We'll await the receipt from all three parties of written submissions in which the documents in question are clearly identified and arguments where they differ relating to each of them, similarly identified. It would appear to the Chamber that five sitting days or let us say a week ought to be allowed, Mr. Saxon, for you to prepare your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would allow three days beyond that to Mr. Mettraux and Mr. Apostolski. You know essentially what is put against you, but three additional days in case something new emerges in the written submissions. So a week to Mr. Saxon and ten days from now for Mr. Mettraux and Mr. Apostolski with their written submissions. Should there be anything entirely novel in the submissions against you, Mr. Saxon, you can have two days beyond that. But we would not anticipate that you will need to respond. We will reserve our decision, of course, on the motion in light of those matters. This seems to be an appropriate time to have the break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are we ready now for the next witness, do you think, Mr. Saxon. Oh, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. At this point the Prosecution will be called witness Eli Cakar. Who is witness M-0160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. There are no protective measures, are there?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked by the interpreters to mind the microphone and not cover it by evidence or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please take the card that is given to you and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. First, may we apologise that you were brought into court and then had to leave again. There were some issues of significance which were being raised with the Court and they were being dealt with. So we welcome you back again. Now I think Mr. Dobbyn has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam, is your name Eli Cakar?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you a Macedonian citizen?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in August 2001, were you working as a television reporter?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And previously have you given statements to members of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you recall on Sunday, the 16th of September, signing another statement that effectively consolidated your prior statements?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance, I would like to show Ms. Cakar the document which bears ERN N006-5034, N006-5050. Ms. Cakar, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Is your signature there at the bottom of page one?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can you look -- take a look at each page in the document and tell us whether you signed each page at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you turn now to page 15, please. Are you on page 15?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you see a paragraph with the title in English witness acknowledgment? And can you tell us whether that is your signature at the bottom of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, after signing that consolidated statement on Sunday, the 16th of September, did you then make some additions or corrections to that statement?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: After I signed it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: On -- yes.

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you make any additions or corrections to that statement on the 16th of September?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes. There were some corrections that were more of a technical nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And were those corrections recorded in a separate document, also dated 16 September 2007?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could I please have the usher's assistance again to show the witness the next document, which has the ERN N006-5051, N006-5056. Ms. Cakar, do you see your signature at the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And did you sign every page of this document at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could you turn to page 5, where, again, you will see a paragraph entitled witness acknowledgment. And can you tell us whether that's your signature at the bottom, under that paragraph. Do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And together, would this consolidated statement and the addendum accurately reflect what you would say if you were to testify orally?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: At this point, Your Honours, I would seek to tender Ms. Cakar's consolidated witness statement and the addendum thereto pursuant to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Ah, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the English addendum to the consolidated list has some comments on the evidence. In line with your decision, the comments should not be admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in our submission we have asked that those comments not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I certainly haven't seen them. You can be assured of that, Ms. Residovic. The document -- the statement and the corrections will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Cakar, in paragraph 6 of your consolidated statement, you refer to a video-clip that you produced and which was shot in the Ljuboten area on 12th August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And at this time I would like to show the witness is a video which is 65 ter 309 with ERN V000-3494, and I would like to show the clip running from 4 minutes and 35 seconds until 7 minutes and 56 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can we stop it here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Cakar, is that your voice that can be heard on the video-clip?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can we continue playing the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Cakar, in paragraph 25 of your consolidated statement, you described your cameraman recording some weapons and being told by Minister Boskoski that: "These are the weapons that we took from the arrested terrorists." Are the weapons that you have just seen on the video the weapons that you referred to in paragraph 25 of your consolidated statement?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I'm not sure at this moment whether Minister Boskoski said it, but from some people that were there, we were explained that this was the weapon that was seized from the terrorists. And that is -- these are the weapons that were recorded by the cameraman.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So just to clarify, these are in fact the weapons that you refer to in paragraph 25 of your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Let me just see. These are the weapons that were seized from the terrorists and it was shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could continue playing the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And stop it there. Sorry, can we just go back to 6 minutes and 25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we play it from there, perhaps, and stop it. There. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Cakar, do you recognise anyone on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I recognise Minister Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And is that the figure in the centre of the picture pointing up into the sky?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And where exactly was Minister Boskoski when he was captured on film here?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: He was in the yard of one of the houses that were outside of the village of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could continue playing the video-clip until the end, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Cakar, is the video-clip that we've just seen the video that you referred to in your consolidated statement, the video that your cameraman shot and that you produced in relation to the events in Ljuboten on 12th August 2001?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: That is the video material that was shot by the cameraman. I don't know whether your question refers to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you produce this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: It was shot by the cameraman of the Macedonian Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Cakar, is this the video that you refer to your consolidated statement?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Oh, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, regarding the proposal that was just given by the Prosecutor, I would like to mention that the video material that was shot by the cameraman of the Macedonian Television was shown to the witness Peter Bouckaert, and it is admitted as P363 MFI. It is true that that material does not contain a Macedonian text that we saw in this material, and the logo of the Macedonian Television but we would like for the Prosecutor to explain us in what relation is this P633, which was shown to Bouckaert and whether the current video-clip would receive a number to avoid a possible confusion about two identical video recordings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can clarify. The video-clip that was shown to Mr. Bouckaert was a clip from a longer video. The longer video also includes a clip that is very similar to this one, but the clip that was marked for identification is a completely different video to the one that has been shown here. It is a video of an interview with Minister Boskoski, not the parts that we've just been shown here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This video will be received as a distinct exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, in the previous paragraph it should say P363 instead of P633.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me just mention that -- that the witness Bouckaert was shown a video and that is registered as P363 MFI and we would like that the Prosecutor sees that video recording and that does not refer to any statement of Minister Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Both counsel seem to be in clear agreement over one thing: For our material purposes, the two videos are identical. We will receive this one. The other is marked for identification if there is any dispute concerning the evidence of Mr. Bouckaert. But the other one is not an exhibit in evidence in the trial. Carry on, please, Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Cakar, do you know of a location known as Brace's house?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: If you can please repeat the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you know of a location that is known by the name of Brace's house?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I just learned about that. In the statements that I saw with the -- with your investigator, I recently learned that that location is called like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And the location that you came to be -- you came to know as being called Brace's house, were you at that location on 12th August 2001?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in your consolidate the statement, you describe spending some time in the yard of a house in the presence of Minister Boskoski from where your cameraman shot much of the video footage. Was this the place that you have since learned was known as Brace's house?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: What we just saw in the video-clip, that was the yard I was in on 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And that was the yard where Minister Boskoski was also. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, could we show what's just been admitted as Exhibit P441, the consolidated statement. And if we could go to paragraph 22, which is on page 9 of the English version, page 10 of the Macedonian version. Ms. Cakar, if you look at paragraph 22, do you see where you state: "On my way out, I saw a group of people, who, according to the minister, are going to be immediately sent to a police station. I think he mentioned the police station Avtokomanda. According to Minister Boskoski, these people were arrested during the action." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I do. And if I may add something, during my statement, I mentioned that I didn't see because I was running and with the angle of my eye I somehow noticed the presence of people. And on several occasions I insisted that it is noted in that way. So I cannot say absolutely whether I have seen something, but somehow with the angle of my eyes, somehow I think -- I think I was aware that there were some people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, these people that you became aware of, could you describe exactly where they were located?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: When we exited the yard through the door, I think there were some people on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And how far from the door were they?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Cakar, if you were shown a map that you drew, would that help refresh your recollection as to the location of these people? Sorry, I'll ask that again. If you were shown a map that you drew in the presence of an Office of the Prosecutor investigator would that help refresh your recollection as to where these people were located?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I can only tell you that after I left at the door, I just ran towards the parked vehicle, and I never turned my head towards there. I just have a feeling that somehow with the angle of my eye I saw some people, but I never turned my head and I didn't look into that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: With the usher assistance, I would like to show Ms. Cakar a map, a sketch that she drew on -- it's dated 30th November, 2003. It is -- it was attached to the consolidated statement but we are not seeking to admit it. Ms. Cakar, do you see towards the bottom on the left-hand side there's a heading Brace's house with a sketch underneath it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't me who draw this sketch, but it was drawn upon my instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you see that in the middle of the page there are the words "arrested people," with an arrow, one pointing up, one pointing down. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Could you assist me? I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: In middle of the page, there are two words written in English, "arrested people." From there, there are two arrows: One going upwards on the page, one going downwards. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And then on the lower sketch do you see the words "three to four metres." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: A bit more difficult to see from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Perhaps if you look at the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I see what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So does this refresh your recollection as to how far away from you these people were located when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Where was Minister Boskoski when he told that you these people had been arrested during the action?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: The minister gave me general informations in the yard before we left, but at that moment I did not know about what people he was speaking about in general. I just received some general information before we left that terrorists have entered from Kosovo, that there was an action, and that people are arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If you could look at paragraph 22 of your statement, please. And if we could go over to the next page where paragraph 22 carries on. The first full sentence on that page of the statement that you signed says: "According to Minister Boskoski, these people were arrested during the action." And in this paragraph you were talking about the group of people outside the gate. So can you tell us where Minister Boskoski was when he told you that these people had been arrested during the action?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Minister Boskoski was not that specific. However, my assumption was that he was talking about these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, you left the yard with Minister Boskoski, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So he left through the same gate as you did?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you caught a glimpse of this group of people there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I already told you I did not see those people but I was aware that there were some people standing around, because I was running.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was Minister Boskoski running?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Taking into account what had you been told and where these people were located, was it your impression that Minister Boskoski knew these people were there?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 25 of your statement, you are refer to some weapons that -- that you filmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: You state there: "The weapons shown in the video were placed close to the car I was using for my way back to Skopje. I think it was placed on the left side of the sidewalk of the road in the direction of Skopje. This was the place where the cameraman recorded the weapons. Minister Boskoski told me, These are the weapons that we took from the arrested terrorists." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Who actually showed you these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I was in the car when the cameraman was filming the weapons, and I don't remember precisely whether some people maybe who were around there with the minister who showed them. So they were left on the road a bit lower from the house in the direction towards Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: When you were seated in the car and your cameraman was filming these weapons, where was Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Where was the minister when he told you, These are the weapons that we took from the arrested terrorists?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Here in the statement things are being written as it was a direct speech of the minister. When we were discussing this with the investigator, I was not in a situation. I could not remember everything specifically so that I would be able to formulate this and to quote somebody. Everything was -- was paraphrased. So as it is written here it is very precise and at this particular moment I cannot be quite sure. Even at the moment when I was providing my statement, I was not able with 100 per cent preciseness to formulate the wording so that they can be placed in the statement as a quote. Back then, I received information that these were weapons that have been seized by -- from the arrested terrorists. This is what I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: But you did read the statement, review it and then sign it. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes. However, when I was giving my statements, on couple of occasions, and during the preparation of the consolidated statement, I was pointing out these things on several occasions, and although at that time maybe -- it was not so important to be so precise. However, I insisted on people being precise, and maybe we had certain problems with the translation, because maybe I was misunderstood, because I tried and I insisted on preciseness throughout the procedure. And maybe I was not aware about the context, maybe. For the investigator, the preciseness was not so important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Well, your precision is appreciated, and I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dobbyn. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Cakar. My name is Edina Residovic and together with my colleague Guenael Mettraux, we represent Mr. Ljube Boskoski. I will kindly ask you to answer several questions of mine, but before I ask you the questions, I will ask you to pay attention for the benefit of the interpretation. Namely, I guess that you understand the language that I am using, and I understand the language that you speak. However, my question and your answer have to be interpreted so that the Honourable judges and our learned colleagues in the courtroom can hear and understand the question and your response; and that is why I kindly ask you, Ms. Cakar, to wait for my question to be interpreted and respond to the question only then. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were born in Strumice in the Republic of Macedonia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have completed the studies of journalism. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have graduated in 1987 and you started working at the Macedonian Radio and TV station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From 1987 to 1987 you were volunteering and in 1989, you were employed with a full-time job. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long did you work at the Macedonian TV and radio?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I was working there until January 2004, 12th of January, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you work at present?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Now I work at the ministry of local self-government.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct, Ms. Cakar, that when you started working for the Macedonian TV and radio, first of all, three years you were working for a programme that was treating the problems in the local communities in the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I was working in the so-called Skopska programme as it was called back then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Afterwards for several years you have been working as a reporter in the Macedonian parliament. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes, around ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in 2001, you were working as a reporter from the Macedonian parliament. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During this period, in 2001, was the crisis period in the Republic of Macedonia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Having in mind the crisis period, there were certain changes in the editorial policy of the Macedonian Radio and TV which was supposed to refer or relate to the issues of that crisis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I did not -- I didn't understand your question well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the crisis at that time in the Republic of Macedonia, is it correct that there were certain changes in the editorial policy and the editors have issued additional tasks or requests from the reporters and journalists?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And those changes in fact were closely related to the crisis itself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes. In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, until that August 2001, you were lucky enough and you could fulfil your tasks of a reporter from the parliament and you did not go to the crisis regions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: I used to go previously as well, but I was not part of the first field team. I was going there if there was a need, if there were plenty of events, plenty of incidents I would go there and if we did not have enough staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you testified that on the 12th of August, your editor-in-chief told you that you were supposed to go to the field for a particular task.

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague just showed you the video footage that was filmed by your colleague, the cameraman, this particular day where -- when you were in the courtyard of the house for which you found out later on that it was called Brace's house. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before this day, you were never present at this particular location where this footage was recorded. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELI CAKAR
utterances.text: Yes.
